articles.title: Indigenous leaders give the UN a roadmap for protecting their peoples
articles.content:
This story is published through the Indigenous News Alliance.



Indigenous communities around the world face mounting, and colliding, impacts from climate change, violence, rising threats from artificial intelligence, and many other crises. Their leaders are demanding that the world take action, and they’ve given the United Nations a 12-point plan for what they say it must do.

Simply put, their proposal calls on the U.N. and governments around the world to take sweeping and rapid action to protect Indigenous land, rights, and lives.

“Our communities — our women, our children, our families — they have a right to action and that’s what we’re not seeing globally,” said Cora McGuire-Cyrette, who is a member of the Bingwi Neyaashi Anishinaabek and spoke on behalf of the Ontario Native Women’s Association. “We’re looking for action.”

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Last week, the seven Indigenous members of the United Nations Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, or EMRIP, finalized the proposal it will present to the U.N. Human Rights Council. But even as the recommendations generated hope for change, the financial crisis facing EMRIP cast a shadow over the proceedings. Many delegates expressed concerns about the future of the forum, and other hard-won international platforms for Indigenous voices.

Given the scale of threats Indigenous peoples face, these forums are more important than ever, said Sheryl Lightfoot, who is Anishinaabe and serves as EMRIP’s North America region expert. “There’s clearly no shortage of work,” she said.

The breadth of the 12 recommendations reflects that urgency, calling for stronger protections for Indigenous cultures and rights and a greater voice in global affairs.

One recommendation sought greater protections for remote Indigenous peoples living in voluntary isolation or initial contact. Others stressed the need to preserve Indigenous languages and data sovereignty.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Delegates also argued that the legal standing of Indigenous peoples must be strengthened by recognizing their rights as distinct from broader human rights and by fully implementing the U.N. Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. They also called on the U.N. to increase Indigenous participation within the Human Rights Council and encourage member states to engage more fully with EMRIP.

Albert Barume is the U.N. special rapporteur on the rights of Indigenous peoples and EMRIP’s former chairperson. He told the delegates about what he called a widespread trend of “stagnation and regression” for human rights. “In the last years,” he said, “almost no single states have taken a new measure protecting Indigenous peoples’ rights. And states that had legal and policy frameworks are actively dismantling and regressing.”

Macy Duxfield, who is Māori and belongs to the Ngaa Rauru, Te Ātihaunui-a-Papārangi, and Ngāi Tahu nations, described Aotearoa New Zealand’s policies toward Indigenous peoples as regressive. But she reminds herself of the continual work that’s still needed to overcome the challenges her people face. “We exist in this moment,” she said. “We’ve inherited the work from our ancestors, and we pass it on to our descendants.”

McGuire-Cyrette and others also reminded delegates about the importance of greater autonomy for Indigenous women and girls. “We recommend the inclusion of Indigenous women in all decisions that impact our lives, our families, and our nations,” McGuire-Cyrette said.

But even as Indigenous delegates try to use international forums to fight for change, those mechanisms are in danger. EMRIP is among the three U.N. bodies focused on Indigenous peoples — along with the Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues and the special rapporteur on the rights of Indigenous peoples. All three agencies face an uncertain future due to dwindling financial support.

Marjolaine Étienne, who is Innu from the Pekuakamiulnuatsh community of Mashteuiatsh in Quebec, told delegates the U.N. Voluntary Fund for Indigenous Peoples needs greater support. The program helps Indigenous representatives cover the costs of attending international meetings. The number of representatives the fund supports is already perilously low, she said. Without greater state contributions, fewer delegates will be able to attend those forums, sidelining them from the international stage.

Just eight countries contribute to the fund, and its budget is less than $2 million. Only three countries contributed to the U.N. Trust Fund for Indigenous Peoples. The United States does not contribute to either of them.

“The liquidity crisis must not be used as an excuse to limit the mandate of EMRIP and to reduce the frequency or depth of country engagements or follow-up,” McGuire-Cyrette said.

Lightfoot acknowledged there is widespread uncertainty within EMRIP and all U.N. bodies amid the agency-wide reform effort known as UN80. But she said EMRIP is preparing for whatever happens. “There are a lot of unanswered questions right now” about the reforms, she said, “and what the impacts of that might be for Indigenous-specific mechanisms.”

“I don’t know where we’re going,” she said. “I don’t know what kind of efficiencies the U.N. will ask of us. But I know we are thinking it through because we want to be ready to respond.”

articles.personality_title: Indigenous leaders present a 12-point plan to the UN to protect their rights and lands
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Indigenous peoples worldwide face serious problems like climate change, violence, and new threats from technology. They want the world to take strong actions to protect their communities, cultures, and lands.

**What happened** – Last week, seven Indigenous experts from the United Nations Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (EMRIP) created a 12-point plan. This plan asks the UN and governments to act quickly to protect Indigenous rights and lands. They will share this plan with the UN Human Rights Council. Leaders like Cora McGuire-Cyrette and Sheryl Lightfoot spoke about the urgent need for change and the challenges Indigenous peoples face.

**Impact** – The plan is important because it covers many areas like protecting remote Indigenous groups, preserving languages, and giving Indigenous peoples more power in international decisions. It also highlights that some countries are taking fewer steps to protect Indigenous rights, or even reversing progress. The plan calls for stronger legal protections and more support for Indigenous women and girls.

**What's next step** – The Indigenous leaders will present their plan to the UN Human Rights Council and ask countries to support it. However, the future of EMRIP and other UN groups that focus on Indigenous issues is uncertain because of money problems. Without enough funding, fewer Indigenous representatives can attend important meetings. The leaders are preparing for changes and hope for more support from countries worldwide.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Indigenous leaders have created a detailed plan asking the UN to take urgent and stronger actions to protect their rights, cultures, and lands amid growing global challenges.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les dirigeants autochtones présentent un plan en 12 points à l'ONU pour protéger leurs droits et leurs terres
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les peuples autochtones du monde entier font face à de graves problèmes comme le changement climatique, la violence et de nouvelles menaces technologiques. Ils demandent au monde d’agir rapidement pour protéger leurs communautés, leurs cultures et leurs terres.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – La semaine dernière, sept experts autochtones du Mécanisme d'experts des Nations Unies sur les droits des peuples autochtones (EMRIP) ont élaboré un plan en 12 points. Ce plan demande à l’ONU et aux gouvernements d’agir vite pour protéger les droits et les terres des autochtones. Ils vont présenter ce plan au Conseil des droits de l’homme de l’ONU. Des dirigeants comme Cora McGuire-Cyrette et Sheryl Lightfoot ont souligné l’urgence du changement et les défis auxquels font face les peuples autochtones.

**Impact** – Ce plan est important car il couvre plusieurs domaines, comme la protection des groupes autochtones isolés, la préservation des langues et le renforcement de la voix autochtone dans les décisions internationales. Il montre aussi que certains pays reculent sur la protection des droits autochtones. Le plan demande des protections juridiques plus fortes et plus de soutien pour les femmes et filles autochtones.

**Prochaine étape** – Les dirigeants autochtones présenteront leur plan au Conseil des droits de l’homme de l’ONU et demanderont aux pays de le soutenir. Cependant, l’avenir de l’EMRIP et d’autres groupes de l’ONU sur les questions autochtones est incertain à cause de problèmes financiers. Sans assez d’argent, moins de représentants autochtones pourront participer aux réunions importantes. Les dirigeants se préparent aux changements et espèrent un meilleur soutien des pays.

**À retenir en une phrase** – Les dirigeants autochtones ont créé un plan détaillé demandant à l’ONU d’agir rapidement et fortement pour protéger leurs droits, leurs cultures et leurs terres face à des défis mondiaux croissants.
articles.personality_title_es: Líderes indígenas presentan un plan de 12 puntos a la ONU para proteger sus derechos y tierras
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los pueblos indígenas en todo el mundo enfrentan problemas graves como el cambio climático, la violencia y nuevas amenazas tecnológicas. Quieren que el mundo tome acciones fuertes para proteger sus comunidades, culturas y tierras.

**Qué pasó** – La semana pasada, siete expertos indígenas del Mecanismo de Expertos de las Naciones Unidas sobre los Derechos de los Pueblos Indígenas (EMRIP) crearon un plan de 12 puntos. Este plan pide a la ONU y a los gobiernos que actúen rápido para proteger los derechos y tierras indígenas. Presentarán este plan al Consejo de Derechos Humanos de la ONU. Líderes como Cora McGuire-Cyrette y Sheryl Lightfoot hablaron sobre la urgencia del cambio y los desafíos que enfrentan los pueblos indígenas.

**Impacto** – El plan es importante porque abarca muchas áreas, como proteger a grupos indígenas aislados, conservar sus idiomas y darles más voz en decisiones internacionales. También muestra que algunos países están retrocediendo en la protección de derechos indígenas. El plan pide protecciones legales más fuertes y más apoyo para mujeres y niñas indígenas.

**Próximo paso** – Los líderes indígenas presentarán su plan al Consejo de Derechos Humanos de la ONU y pedirán apoyo de los países. Sin embargo, el futuro de EMRIP y otros grupos de la ONU que se enfocan en temas indígenas es incierto por problemas de dinero. Sin suficiente financiamiento, menos representantes indígenas podrán asistir a reuniones importantes. Los líderes se están preparando para cambios y esperan más apoyo de los países.

**Resumen en una frase** – Los líderes indígenas han creado un plan detallado que pide a la ONU tomar acciones urgentes y fuertes para proteger sus derechos, culturas y tierras frente a crecientes desafíos globales.

articles.title: ADHD has rewired the workplace. This is what it means for bosses and workers
articles.summary: As ADHD diagnoses have risen, have workplaces caught up with the needs of the workforce?
articles.content:
Taking one of the UK's biggest grocery chains to an employment tribunal was something that Ryan Toghill says almost took over his life.

"It was all I could think about for 18 months and more," he says.

The deputy store manager at Lidl, who'd told his bosses he'd been diagnosed with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), was called to a disciplinary meeting after breaking company rules by using equipment he hadn't been trained to use. After that meeting, Ryan was dismissed for gross misconduct.

He successfully appealed the decision and was offered a lower-paid role. He rejected it and took his case to a tribunal. Eventually, he was awarded more than £45,000 when the judge found his former employer hadn't fully taken his ADHD diagnosis into account during the disciplinary process.

The judgement found reasonable adjustments during the process hadn't been offered to him, such as additional breaks.

He'd been described by a manager as showing "a lack of remorse," something the tribunal found was clearly linked with his communication differences associated with having ADHD.

"I don't show a lot of emotions," Ryan explains. "I could be incredibly happy, angry, upset, or remorseful, and my facial expressions and tone of voice would essentially remain the same."

The tribunal upheld part of his claims for unfair dismissal, wrongful dismissal and a failure to make reasonable adjustments. Lidl says it's "committed to ensuring that everyone receives the reasonable adjustments, clear communication and support they need to thrive."

Campaigners, lawyers and HR teams say cases like this highlight a shift that businesses should be paying attention to.

Thousands of people have been diagnosed as neurodivergent in the last few years, an umbrella term that covers autism, ADHD and other conditions such as dyslexia and Tourette's syndrome.

Since the pandemic in particular, diagnosis rates for ADHD and autism have been rising, and they're featuring more regularly in disputes in employment tribunals.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a significant legal and social advancement in workplace rights for neurodivergent individuals, specifically those with ADHD. The successful tribunal case sets a precedent for reasonable adjustments and fair treatment, which can broadly improve workplace inclusivity and support for many people with neurodivergent conditions. The story is focused, detailed, and has meaningful real-world impact beyond a niche audience.
articles.personality_title: ADHD diagnosis leads to fairer workplace treatment after legal win
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – More people are being diagnosed with ADHD and other neurodivergent conditions like autism and dyslexia. These conditions affect how people think and behave. Since the pandemic, more cases have appeared in workplace disputes.

**What happened** – Ryan Toghill, a deputy store manager at a large UK grocery chain, was dismissed after breaking rules. He had told his bosses about his ADHD diagnosis, but the company didn’t make special adjustments for him during the disciplinary process. Ryan took the company to a tribunal, which found that the employer didn’t treat him fairly because of his ADHD. He won the case and was awarded over £45,000.

**Impact** – This case shows that workplaces need to better understand and support people with ADHD. Employers must make reasonable changes, like extra breaks or clear communication, to help workers with different needs. The tribunal recognized that Ryan’s way of showing emotions was affected by ADHD, which helped explain misunderstandings.

**What’s next step** – More companies may review their rules and training to support neurodivergent workers better. Legal cases like Ryan’s encourage workplaces to create fairer environments and avoid similar problems in the future.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A legal ruling for a worker with ADHD highlights the importance of fair treatment and adjustments in the workplace for neurodivergent employees.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un diagnostic de TDAH entraîne un traitement plus juste au travail après une victoire juridique
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – De plus en plus de personnes sont diagnostiquées avec le TDAH et d'autres conditions neurodivergentes comme l'autisme et la dyslexie. Ces conditions influencent la façon dont les gens pensent et se comportent. Depuis la pandémie, ces cas apparaissent plus souvent dans les conflits au travail.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Ryan Toghill, directeur adjoint dans une grande chaîne de supermarchés au Royaume-Uni, a été licencié après avoir enfreint des règles. Il avait informé ses employeurs de son diagnostic de TDAH, mais l’entreprise n’a pas fait d’aménagements spéciaux pour lui pendant la procédure disciplinaire. Ryan a porté l’affaire devant un tribunal, qui a jugé que l’employeur ne l’avait pas traité équitablement à cause de son TDAH. Il a gagné et a reçu plus de 45 000 £.

**Impact** – Cette affaire montre que les lieux de travail doivent mieux comprendre et soutenir les personnes atteintes de TDAH. Les employeurs doivent faire des changements raisonnables, comme des pauses supplémentaires ou une communication claire, pour aider les employés avec des besoins différents. Le tribunal a reconnu que la manière dont Ryan exprime ses émotions était affectée par le TDAH, ce qui a aidé à expliquer les malentendus.

**Prochaine étape** – Plus d’entreprises pourraient revoir leurs règles et formations pour mieux soutenir les travailleurs neurodivergents. Des cas juridiques comme celui de Ryan encouragent les lieux de travail à être plus justes et à éviter ce genre de problèmes.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Un jugement légal en faveur d’un travailleur atteint de TDAH souligne l’importance d’un traitement équitable et d’aménagements adaptés pour les employés neurodivergents.
articles.personality_title_es: Un diagnóstico de TDAH conduce a un trato más justo en el trabajo tras victoria legal
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Cada vez más personas reciben diagnósticos de TDAH y otras condiciones neurodivergentes como el autismo y la dislexia. Estas condiciones afectan cómo piensan y se comportan las personas. Desde la pandemia, estos casos aparecen más en disputas laborales.

**Qué pasó** – Ryan Toghill, subgerente en una gran cadena de supermercados del Reino Unido, fue despedido tras romper reglas. Había informado a sus jefes sobre su diagnóstico de TDAH, pero la empresa no hizo ajustes especiales para él durante el proceso disciplinario. Ryan llevó el caso a un tribunal, que determinó que el empleador no lo trató justamente por su TDAH. Ryan ganó y recibió más de £45,000.

**Impacto** – Este caso muestra que los lugares de trabajo deben entender mejor y apoyar a personas con TDAH. Los empleadores deben hacer cambios razonables, como pausas extras o comunicación clara, para ayudar a empleados con necesidades diferentes. El tribunal reconoció que la forma en que Ryan muestra emociones está afectada por su TDAH, lo que ayudó a aclarar malentendidos.

**Próximo paso** – Más empresas podrían revisar sus reglas y capacitaciones para apoyar mejor a trabajadores neurodivergentes. Casos legales como el de Ryan animan a los lugares de trabajo a ser más justos y evitar problemas similares.

**Resumen en una frase** – Un fallo legal a favor de un trabajador con TDAH resalta la importancia de un trato justo y ajustes adecuados para empleados neurodivergentes.
